conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—EPDS for short. It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, because mood changes are incredibly common after childbirth and you deserve support if things feel heavy or off.  

Everything you share stays confidential between you and your care team, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. We’ll go through ten gentle questions about the past seven days; each one usually takes only a moment to answer, and we can pause anytime you need.  

Whenever you’re ready, we’ll begin.  

First question: Over the last week, have you still been able to look forward to things, or has the enjoyment slipped away?

I still get excited about some things—like when my mom brings over dinner or when the baby gives me one of those gummy smiles—but it’s not the same spark I had before. It feels like the color’s been turned down a notch on everything I used to love.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Most days I can still laugh—like yesterday when my husband made that silly face changing the diaper—but the giggles fade faster than they used to. Sometimes I’ll smile and realize I’m forcing it, so it doesn’t feel as easy or natural anymore.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still mark little things on the calendar—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park—but when the moment comes it feels kind of flat, like I’m going through the motions more than actually tasting the muffin or feeling the sun. I wouldn’t say I dread activities, I just don’t get that little lift I used to; it’s more “okay, this is nice” than “I can’t wait.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Like, if the baby won’t settle, I immediately think it must be something I ate or that I’m not soothing him right. A couple nights ago he was fussy for an hour and I kept replaying every little thing I’d done that day, sure I’d messed up somehow. It’s not constant, but when I’m tired it’s the first place my brain goes.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I’ll be feeding her and my mind just starts spinning—what if she’s not getting enough milk, what if I miss some sign she’s sick, what if I’m doing this whole mom thing wrong. Nothing’s actually happening, but my chest feels tight until I check her a million times or Google stuff. I can usually calm myself down, but it’s like a little alarm goes off for no real reason.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not full panic, but every so often—like when I’m alone with her at night—I get this sudden rush of “what if something happens and I can’t handle it?” My heart beats faster and I feel shaky for a few minutes, then it passes once I tell myself we’re safe. It’s not every day, maybe two or three times this week, and I can talk myself down, but it still catches me off guard.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days it feels like the laundry and the dishes and the night feeds just pile up faster than I can handle them. I’ll be rocking the baby and thinking about the million things I still need to do, and my stomach gets all tight. I usually push through and check things off once she naps, but it’s like I’m constantly playing catch-up and I end the day totally drained.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I wouldn’t say I’m lying there miserable, but I do toss and turn some nights. Once the baby’s down, my brain starts replaying everything I think I did wrong, and it takes me a while to shut it off. I usually get to sleep within half an hour, but a couple nights this week I was still awake after an hour and a half, just staring at the ceiling.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah, I’ve had moments—mostly in the evenings—where I just feel this heavy sadness settle in. It’s not every day, but maybe four or five times this week I’ll suddenly feel like I could cry, even if nothing bad happened. It lifts after a while, especially if I talk to my husband, but in those minutes it feels like I’m carrying extra weight on my chest.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve cried a couple of times—once on Tuesday when the baby wouldn’t nap and I felt like I was failing, and again yesterday when I dropped the pumped milk on the floor. It wasn’t all day sobbing, just sudden tears that came and went, maybe ten minutes each time.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I get overwhelmed sometimes, but I haven’t thought about hurting myself, not at all.

You've shared that while you can still laugh and look forward to small outings, the joy feels muted-<quote>the colour's been turned down</quote>-and you're often running on empty. You describe sudden tears, tight-chested worry about your baby's health, racing thoughts at bedtime, and a heavy sadness that settles in most evenings, yet you continue to push through daily tasks and remain committed to caring for your little one.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 16, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent self-blame that occurs 'some of the time' when things go wrong, matching 'Yes, some of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent, intrusive worries about infant care that arise without objective cause, consistent with "Yes, sometimes" anxiety.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes episodic sudden fear with physical symptoms (racing heart, shakiness) that she must actively self-soothe; frequency of 2–3 times in the past week maps to "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent overwhelm and physical tension but still manages tasks, aligning with "sometimes not coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes occasional trouble falling asleep due to racing thoughts, but not nightly or severe insomnia.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intense sadness 4-5 times in a week with physical heaviness, aligning with "Yes, quite often."</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total ≥14 indicates probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>. Your score of 16 meets this threshold, with prominent <sym>anhedonia</sym> (Q2=2), <sym>excessive guilt</sym> (Q3=2), <sym>generalised anxiety</sym> (Q4=2), <sym>panic-like symptoms</sym> (Q5=2), <sym>feeling overwhelmed</sym> (Q6=2), <sym>sleep disturbance</sym> linked to rumination (Q7=2), and frequent <sym>low mood</sym> with crying (Q8=2, Q9=1). These symptoms align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most days, markedly diminished interest, fatigue, guilt, and anxiety persisting beyond two weeks postpartum. Absence of self-harm thoughts (Q10=0) is reassuring yet does not negate clinical severity. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent follow-up with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>obstetrician</med> to discuss mood and anxiety since delivery
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med>, peer support groups, or <med>sertraline</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Practice 15-20 minutes of protected rest or mindfulness when baby naps; enlist partner or family for one nightly bottle or chore shift to improve sleep continuity
4. Schedule re-screen with this office in 1-2 weeks to track symptom trajectory and treatment response
5. Keep national 24/7 <med>Maternal Mental Health Hotline</med> 1-833-943-5746 in your phone for after-hours support
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 16: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient-reported symptoms (2 wks postpartum):

Affect/mood  
- Episodic tearfulness, “heavy sadness,” diminished pleasure/enjoyment in previously pleasant activities  
- Able to laugh intermittently, but describes laughter as “forced” and transient  

Cognitive themes  
- Self-blame (“I must be doing something wrong”) when infant fussy  
- Ruminative review of perceived maternal failures at night, prolonging sleep onset  

Anxiety/overwhelm  
- Unprompted worry about infant health, milk intake, own competence  
- Two to three brief nocturnal episodes of heightened autonomic arousal (racing heart, shakiness) without objective trigger; self-resolving  
- Daily sense of being “behind,” tight stomach, end-of-day exhaustion

Sleep  
- Initial insomnia 2–3 nights/week linked to ruminative thoughts; usual sleep onset ≤30 min, occasionally 90 min

Safety  
- Denies any thoughts of self-harm; no suicidal ideation endorsed

Pattern summary  
Responses indicate sub-syndromal depressive symptoms and prominent anxiety/worry that exceed typical new-parent concerns; functional impact apparent in emotional fatigue, sleep disruption, and reduced enjoyment. No current safety risk identified. Re-screen in 1–2 weeks or sooner if symptoms escalate; consider formal evaluation for perinatal depression/anxiety if persistence or worsening.
